subject: Climate & Environment
title: Particulate Matter Explained
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Particulate Matter Explained.

hook.text: The deadliest air pollutant is invisible. Particles 30 times thinner than a human hair.

buildup.text: PM2.5 — particles under 2.5 micrometers — slip past your nose and lungs into your blood.

discovery.text: They come from car exhaust, power plants, cooking fires, and even desert dust.

twist.text: There is no safe level. Even low concentrations increase heart attack and stroke risk.

climax.text: PM2.5 kills an estimated 4.2 million people every year — more than malaria and HIV combined.

punchline.text: The most dangerous thing in the air is too small to see.

quiz.question: What makes PM2.5 so dangerous?
options: Particles are small enough to enter the bloodstream

details.summary: Particulate matter refers to tiny solid or liquid particles suspended in air that penetrate deep into lungs and even enter the bloodstream. PM2.5, particles under 2.5 micrometers, is the most dangerous class, responsible for millions of premature deaths annually worldwide.
details.whyItMatters: PM2.5 is the leading environmental cause of death globally. Knowing what it is helps you interpret air-quality readings and protect your health.
takeaways: PM2.5 particles are small enough to pass into the bloodstream
Sources include vehicle exhaust, power plants, and cooking fires
No concentration level has been found to be completely safe

faq.question: What is the difference between PM2.5 and PM10?
faq.answer: PM10 includes particles up to 10 micrometers such as dust and pollen that mostly lodge in the nose and throat. PM2.5 particles are under 2.5 micrometers and penetrate deep into lung tissue and the bloodstream, causing greater cardiovascular and respiratory harm.

faq.question: How many deaths does PM2.5 cause each year?
faq.answer: The World Health Organization estimates PM2.5 exposure causes roughly 4.2 million premature deaths per year from heart disease, stroke, lung cancer, and respiratory infections, making it the deadliest air pollutant.
